Financial education programs use several active engagement strategies to involve parents, with the evidence pointing to three main approaches: interactive and experiential methods, parent-child co-learning activities, and digital/hybrid delivery formats.

Interactive and experiential methods are central to many financial education resources. The evidence includes examples of “fun games and activities” designed to introduce children to financial topics, described as engaging and already structured for educators [N1-R1]. Apple Federal Credit Union also highlights “ten engaging tools and activities” for teaching children about money management [N1-R2], while Sesame Workshop emphasizes resources and activities for starting financial education early and talking to children during tough financial situations [N1-R3]. These sources support the idea that games, activities, and structured lessons are used to make learning experiential rather than purely informational.

Parent-child co-learning activities are also emphasized in the evidence. CEE’s family engagement resources explicitly state that programs are designed so families can become financially savvy together [N1-R5], which aligns with the concept of merging teaching with family routines. The same evidence set also points to “hands-on family engagement strategies for schools” paired with programs, suggesting that learning is not limited to school settings but can occur through home-based or family-connected activities [N1-R4]. This supports the claim that financial learning is often embedded into everyday routines rather than treated as an isolated lesson.

Digital and hybrid delivery methods are another key strategy. Banzai’s free financial literacy classes are described as interactive and online, targeted at teachers, parents, and financial institutions [N3-R1]. FitMoney similarly positions itself as offering parents and caregivers innovative digital platforms and at-home activities, while also empowering teachers with a curriculum [N3-R2]. The tearsheet article further notes that collaborative apps and parent-child learning content can transform how families engage with financial education [N3-R5]. Together, these sources show that digital and hybrid formats make participation easier and more accessible, especially by reducing logistical barriers and allowing flexible learning outside school hours.

Overall, the evidence supports a package of active engagement strategies: interactive games and activities, co-learning with children, and digital/hybrid delivery that aligns with parents’ and families’ practical routines and accessibility needs [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].
